findings.title: Debug logging left in at Error level, dumping every ID list on each batch
findings.body: Six `r.log.Error(...)` calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) run unconditionally in the cleanup loop. They log the full `ids` slice, the SQL condition, and an `err` value that is always nil at that point. Each batch emits two Error-level lines, including the final empty batch when there is nothing to clean. With the batch size configurable, the ID list can reach tens of thousands of entries per line. Together with the 1-minute ticker, this floods the error logs and trips alerting on error-level logs even when nothing went wrong. These look like debugging leftovers. Remove them, or log only counts at Debug level.

findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute
findings.body: The cleanup service ticker is changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This is unrelated to the deadlock fix and is not mentioned in the PR description. It looks like a local-testing leftover. It makes every cleanup job (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, short URLs, query history) run 10x more often. The annotation cleanup now runs a SELECT plus a DELETE per batch, so this raises load and contention on the annotation table, the very thing this PR is meant to reduce. It also multiplies the log noise from the Error-level logging. Revert to 10 minutes.

findings.title: Bound-parameter IN list can exceed driver placeholder limits on Postgres/MySQL for large batch sizes
findings.body: Outside SQLite, `deleteByIDs` builds `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (?,?,...)` with one placeholder per ID, so the number of placeholders equals `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize`. Postgres and MySQL prepared statements cap placeholders at 65535. The old query embedded the limit in SQL and used no parameters, so any batch size worked. With this change, a deployment that configures a batch size above that cap will fail every cleanup run with a driver error. The special case only handles SQLite (threshold 999). Chunk the IDs, or inline the integer IDs for all dialects (they are int64, so this is safe).
